title: Some Ālāps in Rāga Yaman
summary: Three Yaman ālāpas marked with Pathak ji's pause signs. Then svasthāna (a fixed note up to its fourth; four across the registers), the guru as cure for doubt, and the marks for rāga outlines: a circle for vādī, a half-circle for saṃvādī, two halves for vivādī, a bar joining paired notes, a snake for oscillation.

blocks.text: Some ālāpas of Rāga Yaman
(1) Ṇi Re Ga + Ṇi Re Ga Ma′ Re Ga + Ṇi Re Ma′ – Ma′ Ga, Ṇi Re Re Ma′ Ga, Pa Ma′ Ga Re Ga, Ṇi Re Ga Ma′ Pa – Re Ga, Ga Re – Ga Re Ṇi Re – Sa|
(2) Ṇi Re Ga Ma′ Pa + Ga Ma′ – GaMa′ Pa, Ga Ma′ Dha Pa, Ṇi Re Ga – Re Re GaMa′ – GaMa′ Dha Pa, PaMa′ GaRe GaMa′ Pa, Pa Re Ga + Ga Re Ṇi Re Sa|
(3) Ga Ma′ Dha Ni – Ni Dha Pa + Ga Ma′ GaMa′ Ni Dha Pa, Ṇi Re – Re Ga – Ga Ma′ Ni Dha – Pa, Pa Ma′ – Re Ma′ Ga + Ga Re Ṇi Re Sa|

Thus it is clear that if, in the group of notes of a nyāsa (resting note), some special feature is shown and it is then given the form of a nyāsa again, that is called vinyāsa (phrase-ending note). Just as there is one sanyāsa (ending note of the first phrase) after many nyāsas, so in the same way there are many vinyāsas in one nyāsa; though they are uttered after the nyāsa, they are regarded as parts of the nyāsa. And apanyāsas (intermediate resting notes) occur anywhere in the middle of any nyāsa. This is the form of ālāpa (slow unmetred elaboration).

blocks.verse:
अचला च्चतूर्थ पर्यन्तम् स्वस्थानम् कथ्यते बुधैः।
मन्द्र मध्यक तारेषु चतुः स्वस्थान योजना।१२१।
blocks.text: The wise call the span from a fixed note up to the fourth note a svasthāna. In the lower, middle and upper registers, four svasthānas are arranged.

The group of notes from a fixed note (acal svara), that is Sa or 'Pa', up to the fourth note is called svasthāna (group from a fixed note up to the fourth). Just as a chariot is understood to be complete with four wheels, an animal or a cot with four legs, and a building with four directions, so four notes are needed for the ālāpa to dwell in. The remaining notes are for its development. That is why, in everyday speech, the word sargam (solfège) [Sa Re Ga Ma] is used so much.

Thus in practice there are four svasthānas across the three registers (saptaka), because the lower register (mandra saptaka) and the upper register (tāra saptaka) are not used in full; only half of each is used. So from Ma or Pa of the lower register up to Sa of the middle register is taken as the first svasthāna; then from middle Sa up to the note Ma the second svasthāna; then from middle Pa up to upper Ṡa the third svasthāna; and from upper Ṡa up to upper Ṁa the fourth svasthāna. In the svara vistāra (elaboration of notes) of any rāga these svasthānas are used in order. But in rāgas whose emphasis lies in the upper register, we cannot follow the order of the svasthānas when elaborating their notes; even so, the svasthāna has to be taken as the basis.

On the basis of the rules above, we are now going to present the svara vistāra (elaboration of notes) of a few rāgas. Rāgas are elaborated still further on the basis of the elements of tāna (tāna tattva). But here I do not wish to elaborate too much. The sādhaka (practitioner) should practise these elaborations sitting in the shade of the guru (teacher), and should sometimes use his own intelligence as well.

blocks.verse:
अज्ञानात् संशयो व्याधिः शास्त्रे तस्यौषधिः स्थिता।
गुरूम् वैध्यम् समाश्रित्य सन्तुष्टः शान्तिमाप्नुयात्।१२२।
blocks.text: Doubt born of ignorance is a disease, and its medicine lies in the śāstra. Taking refuge in the guru as physician, one becomes content and attains peace.

That is, because of ignorance many kinds of doubt arise in the mind. Doubt makes the mind sick. The medicine for this disease of doubt certainly lies in the śāstra (systematic treatise), but only by taking refuge in the physician who is the guru (teacher) can that doubt be removed. When doubt is removed, the mind attains peace.

blocks.verse:
गोला कारे तु वादी स्यात् संवादी त्वर्ध गोलके।
अर्धद्वये विवादीस्या न्निश्चिन्हास्त्वनुवादिनः।१२३।
blocks.text: A note in a circle is the vādī (principal note); one in a half circle is the saṃvādī (consonant second note); one within two halves is the vivādī (dissonant note); and the unmarked notes are the anuvādī (assonant notes).

blocks.verse:
दण्डा कारेण संबद्धौ स्वरौ संगतये मतौ।
सर्प चिन्हाः स्वराः ह्यत्र भवेयुः कम्पिताः सदा।१२४।
blocks.text: Two notes joined by a staff-shaped sign (daṇḍākāra) are meant to go together (saṅgati, companionship of notes). Notes here with the snake sign (sarpa cihna) are always to be oscillated (kampita).

blocks.verse:
तीव्रादीनां तु संकेतः कृतो नारायणैः पुरा।
दृष्ट्वारोहेऽवरोहे च ज्ञातव्यास्ते मनीषिभि।१२५।
blocks.text: The signs for tīvra and the other [altered] notes were made long ago by Nārāyaṇa [Bhātkhaṇḍe ji]. The wise should learn them by seeing them in the ascent and the descent.

In the ślokas above, some symbolic signs for the notes have been given. On the basis of these signs we shall get a general introduction to rāgas through their āroha avaroha (ascent and descent) alone. For a detailed introduction, other śāstras (treatises) of music may be consulted.
(1) Take the note written inside a circle as the vādī (principal note), e.g. - [Ga]
(2) Notes written in a half circle are to be regarded as saṃvādī (consonant second note), e.g. - °Ni
(3) Take notes placed within two half circles as vivādī (dissonant note), e.g. - °Ma°
(4) Where in the ascent we mark Ga Ma Pa Dha in this form, the companionship (saṅgati) of those two notes will be rāga-identifying.
(5) Take the notes that have a snake-like sign beneath them as oscillated (āndolita) in that rāga, e.g. Ga
Apart from these, the signs for tīvra and other notes will be taken from the works of the late Śrī Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇ Bhātkhaṇḍe ji, which were settled long ago.

So if, in the following rāgas, we elaborate the notes keeping in mind the signs marked in the ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent), we shall have greater success in the svara vistāra (elaboration of notes) of the rāga. First of all let us look at Rāga Bhūpālī, which is both sweet and easy on the bansī (bamboo bānsurī).
